title: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
summary: How kernel Rust wraps C APIs: layers and bindings, building and testing modules, Result for errno, locks, ARef and RCU, pinning, lists and work items, C to Rust vtables, bus drivers with Devres, and the limits.
outcomes: Explain why drivers call only safe abstractions, and what bindgen, rust/helpers and the module! macro each generate
Build, load and test a Rust module, and read KUnit results from doctests and #[kunit_tests] suites
Compute which values IS_ERR() treats as errors and trace how to_result and from_err_ptr map C returns to Result
Choose between Mutex, SpinLock and SpinLockIrq, and between Arc, ARef and an RCU guard for an object
Explain why kernel objects must be pinned and read pin_init! code for lists, work items and condition variables
Trace a misc device ioctl from userspace through a Rust trampoline and avoid double fetches with UserSliceReader
Explain how probe, unbind, Devres and Revocable keep a PCI driver from touching device memory after unbind
Identify bugs Rust does not prevent, using the Rust Binder CVE and klint's atomic-context lint as examples

lessons.title: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver

blocks.md:
The C kernel API is full of rules that only humans enforce: take the lock before touching the data, unlock it exactly once on every exit path, never touch an object after dropping its last reference, check `IS_ERR()` (the test for an error code hidden inside a pointer, lesson 3) before dereferencing a returned pointer. Break one and the code still compiles. The bug shows up later as a crash or a security hole.

You know from the C and Rust course that safe Rust turns many of these rules into compile errors. Rust for Linux applies that idea to the kernel. Support was merged in **v6.1** (2022) explicitly as an experiment: was Rust worth its technical, procedural and social cost? At the 2025 Maintainers Summit the experiment was declared concluded, and the patch removing the "experimental" wording says it plainly: Rust is here to stay.

Kernel Rust is `#![no_std]`: it links only `core`, not the standard library. `core` is the part of Rust's library that needs no operating system underneath (basic types, `Option`, `Result`, iterators); `std` adds collections, threads and files that assume one, and inside the kernel there is no operating system below you. There is no `std::vec::Vec` that aborts on allocation failure and no `std::sync::Mutex` built on a userspace futex (fast userspace mutex: the Linux system call that user-space locks sleep on).

The `kernel` crate provides kernel versions instead: `KVec` (a vector) and `KBox` (one heap-owned value, like `Box`), `Arc`, `Mutex`, `SpinLock` (a lock that spins in a loop instead of sleeping while it waits), and `pr_info!` (print to the kernel log).

Every allocating call takes GFP flags and returns a `Result`. GFP stands for "get free pages", the kernel's underlying allocation function, and the flags tell the allocator what it may do to find memory: `GFP_KERNEL` may sleep while memory is reclaimed, `GFP_ATOMIC` must not sleep. When an allocation fails, the `Result` carries the error `ENOMEM` ("error: no memory"), which C code sees as -12.

The interesting design question is where `unsafe` lives. The answer is a strict layering, with one shortcut the kernel docs explicitly forbid.

blocks.title: Who may call what: the Rust layers in the kernel tree

scenes.caption: Start at the bottom. The C kernel exposes its API through headers in include/. Nothing here knows about Rust.
At build time bindgen reads the headers listed in rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h and emits Rust declarations for their functions and types: the bindings crate. Every call into it is unsafe.
bindgen cannot turn C inline functions or non-trivial macros into callable symbols. A tiny C wrapper in rust/helpers/ (for example rust_helper_mutex_lock) fills the gap.

Subsystem abstractions in rust/kernel/ call the bindings inside unsafe blocks, each with a SAFETY comment (why this call cannot cause undefined behavior), and expose a safe API such as Mutex, Arc, KVec or MiscDevice.
A driver (a leaf module) uses only the safe API. If the abstractions are sound, nothing the driver writes in safe code can cause undefined behavior.
The kernel docs mark the shortcut from a driver straight to bindings as forbidden. If an abstraction is missing, the fix is to add it to the subsystem, where it gets reviewed once for everyone.

blocks.md:
Two terms from the kernel docs:

- **Bindings** are Rust declarations of C functions and types, generated by `bindgen` from headers. They are raw: pointers, C integers, no lifetimes. Calling them is `unsafe`.
- **Abstractions** are hand-written Rust in `rust/kernel/` that wrap bindings into an "as safe as possible" API. The docs give the two standard moves: turn C acquire and release into constructors and destructors (`Drop`), and turn C integer error codes into `Result`.

Why helpers? lockdep is the kernel's lock dependency validator: at runtime it records the order in which locks are taken and warns about any order that could deadlock. With lockdep enabled, `include/linux/mutex.h` has `#define mutex_lock(lock) mutex_lock_nested(lock, 0)`. A macro is not a symbol, so `bindgen` has nothing to bind. `rust/helpers/mutex.c` defines a real function `rust_helper_mutex_lock()` that just calls `mutex_lock()`.

Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 10 shows what happens when it fails.

Here is the in-tree minimal module, `samples/rust/rust_minimal.rs` (module parameters and three extra log lines trimmed; lesson 2 runs the full version). Watch for three kernel-specific details: `module!` instead of `module_init()` and `module_exit()` (the C macros that register a module's load and unload functions), fallible allocation with GFP flags, and `Drop` as the exit function, which runs when the module is unloaded (for example by the `rmmod` command).

blocks.title: Loading and unloading rust_minimal

scenes.caption: module! generates the module's init and exit glue and its metadata (name, license, authors). On load, the kernel calls into the generated init, which calls RustMinimal::init.
KVec is the kernel's vector. Every growth takes allocation flags (GFP_KERNEL may sleep) and returns a Result, because a kernel allocation can fail and must not abort the machine.
Each ? either unwraps Ok and continues or returns the error to the caller. On success all three values are in place.
Ok(RustMinimal) hands the module state to the kernel. It lives until the module is unloaded.

Suppose instead the allocation for 200 failed. The third ? returns Err(ENOMEM); the local KVec is dropped (freeing its buffer) and the load fails with -12. No exit code is needed for the half-built state.
Back on the success path, rmmod drops the module state. Drop is the exit function: it runs exactly once, and the KVec frees its buffer afterwards automatically.

My numbers are [72, 108, 200]

blocks.md:
`module!` is the first place in this course where C calls Rust. When a module is loaded, the kernel calls a C-ABI function (one using the C calling convention) named `init_module` that the `.ko` provides, and `cleanup_module` when it is unloaded. The macro generates both, plus a `static` slot for the module state.

`__init` builds `RustMinimal` *in place* in that static through pin-init (lesson 6) and turns an `Err` into a negative errno with `to_errno()` (lesson 3). `__exit` drops the value in the slot, which is what runs your `Drop`. For a module built into the kernel image, the macro instead places a pointer to its init function in an initcall section that the kernel runs at boot.

blocks.caption: Trimmed from the quote! template in rust/macros/module.rs. The real output wraps these items in two nested private modules so nothing else can call them, which is what the SAFETY comments rely on.

blocks.md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

blocks.question: You are writing a Rust driver and need a C function from a subsystem that has no Rust abstraction yet. What does kernel policy expect?
options: Call it through `bindings::` inside an `unsafe` block in the driver, with a SAFETY comment
Add (or extend) a safe abstraction for it in the subsystem's Rust code, and use that from the driver
Rewrite the C function in Rust inside the driver so no FFI is needed
Use `extern "C"` to declare the function by hand in the driver
blocks.explain: The general-information doc says leaf modules such as drivers should not use the C bindings directly; subsystems provide as-safe-as-possible abstractions. Declaring the symbol yourself is the same forbidden shortcut with less checking. Duplicating the C logic would create a second implementation to maintain.

blocks.question: A colleague's build fails: `bindings::spin_lock` does not exist even though `spin_lock()` is used all over the C code. Most likely cause?
options: The bindings crate only includes headers listed in `rust/helpers/`
Rust code may not take spinlocks
`spin_lock` is a macro or inline function in C, so bindgen emits no callable symbol; a `rust/helpers/` wrapper is needed
bindgen only runs when `CLIPPY=1` is set
blocks.explain: bindgen generates declarations for real functions and types it finds in the headers included from `rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h`. For C inline functions and non-trivial macros the docs say to add a small wrapper to `rust/helpers/`, exactly like `rust_helper_mutex_lock`.

lessons.title: Build, load and test a Rust module

blocks.md:
Reading `rust_minimal` is one thing; running it is another. The tiny goal of this lesson: get the line `Rust minimal sample (init)` into a kernel log, then make a test fail on purpose and read what the kernel reports.

A note on what you see here: this course was written without a Linux kernel build environment, so the build and boot commands below come from the kernel's own documentation and were **not run** for this lesson. No build log or `dmesg` output is invented. The only output shown is either quoted from the kernel docs (and labelled so) or produced by a userspace Rust program that was actually run.

First, the toolchain. Building kernel Rust needs `rustc`, the Rust standard library *source* (the build cross-compiles `core` for the kernel target), `bindgen`, and libclang, which bindgen uses to parse C headers. `LLVM=1` tells the kernel build to use the Clang and LLVM tools instead of GCC; the Quick Start calls this the best supported setup and GCC "very experimental".

`make LLVM=1 rustavailable` runs the same check Kconfig (the kernel's configuration system) uses to decide `RUST_IS_AVAILABLE`, and if the answer is no, it says why. Until it passes, `CONFIG_RUST` ("Rust support" under General setup) does not even appear in the menu.

blocks.title: From source tree to a loaded Rust module

scenes.caption: Step 1: rustavailable checks rustc, the Rust library source, bindgen and libclang. If any is missing or unsuitable it prints the reason, and CONFIG_RUST stays hidden.
Step 2: enable Rust support, then Kernel hacking, Sample kernel code, Rust samples, and set the minimal sample to m so it is built as a loadable module.
Step 3: one make builds the kernel image, generates the bindings with bindgen, compiles the kernel crate and the sample, and links rust_minimal.ko.

Step 4: boot that kernel somewhere disposable. virtme-ng (the vng command) boots a freshly built kernel in QEMU (a machine emulator that runs it as a virtual machine) over a copy-on-write view of your own filesystem, so a crash costs nothing.
Step 5: inside the guest, insmod runs the generated init_module; the pr_info! lines go to the kernel log, which dmesg prints. rmmod runs cleanup_module and so the Drop impl.
